items.readable_text:
Content:
We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data [MATH: (x,y).] We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. We call this process polynomial regression.

Content:
The following table gives the number of units [MATH: x] (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits [MATH: y] (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing [MATH: x] units:

Content:
| Goods [MATH: (x)] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| Profit [MATH: (y)] | [MATH: 16] | [MATH: 11] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 18] |

Content:
Suppose we want to find the quadratic function

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2]

Content:
that best fits the given data points.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/151c1d8d5104005ab862cb6ace27196d]

Content:
Substituting the values of [MATH: x] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the following system:

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + 1β_{1} + 1^{2}β_{2} = 16; β_{0} + 2β_{1} + 2^{2}β_{2} = 11; β_{0} + 3β_{1} + 3^{2}β_{2} = 15; β_{0} + 4β_{1} + 4^{2}β_{2} = 18]

Content:
This system can be written using matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|1|1^{2}; 1|2|2^{2}; 1|3|3^{2}; 1|4|4^{2}]]

Content:
where [MATH: X] is the design matrix, [MATH: \boldsymbol{\beta}] is the parameter vector, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0, \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0, \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.

Content:
Notice that this is exactly the least-squares problem for the system [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}.] Therefore, the coefficients of the curve that best fits the data can be found as the solution to the corresponding least-squares problem!

Content:
Pre-multiplying the equation [MATH: X \boldsymbol{\beta} = \mathbf{y}] by [MATH: X^T,] we obtain the corresponding normal equation

Content:
[MATH: X^T \! X {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Since the columns of [MATH: X] are linearly independent, the matrix [MATH: {X^T}X] is invertible, and

Content:
[MATH: {\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}} = (X^T \! X )^{-1} X^T \mathbf{y}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: X] and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] into the formula above and simplifying, we get

Content:
[MATH: β^(^) = [22.5; − 9; 2].]

Content:
Therefore, the quadratic curve of best fit (regression curve) is

Content:
[MATH: y = 22.5 - 9x + 2x^2.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We've seen how to construct a simple linear regression model given some bivariate data [MATH: (x,y).] We can generalize this technique to fit data to an arbitrary polynomial. We call this process polynomial regression.

Content:
The following table gives the number of units [MATH: x] (in hundreds) produced by a small company and the respective profits [MATH: y] (in thousands of dollars) earned for producing [MATH: x] units:

Content:
| Goods [MATH: (x)] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| Profit [MATH: (y)] | [MATH: 16] | [MATH: 11] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 18] |

Content:
Suppose we want to find the quadratic function

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2]

Content:
that best fits the given data points.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/151c1d8d5104005ab862cb6ace27196d]

Content:
Substituting the values of [MATH: x] into the regression equation and equating the results to the corresponding observed values of [MATH: y,] we obtain the following system:

Content:
[MATH: {β_{0} + 1β_{1} + 1^{2}β_{2} = 16; β_{0} + 2β_{1} + 2^{2}β_{2} = 11; β_{0} + 3β_{1} + 3^{2}β_{2} = 15; β_{0} + 4β_{1} + 4^{2}β_{2} = 18]

Content:
This system can be written using matrix notation as

Content:
[MATH: [1|1|1^{2}; 1|2|2^{2}; 1|3|3^{2}; 1|4|4^{2}]]

Content:
where [MATH: X] is the design matrix, [MATH: \boldsymbol{\beta}] is the parameter vector, and [MATH: \mathbf{y}] is the observation vector.

Content:
Since our points do not lie on a quadratic curve, there will be no parameters [MATH: \beta_0, \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] such that this equation is true. So instead, we seek parameters [MATH: \beta_0, \beta_1,] and [MATH: \beta_2] that best approximate the solution.

Content:
In other words, we seek to find a column vector [MATH: \boldsymbol\beta] such that

Content:
[MATH: \| \mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}\|]

Content:
is as small as possible.
